WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congresswoman Frederica S. Wilson (FL-24) introduced the Glaucoma Vision Act of 2026, legislation to expand access to annual glaucoma screenings, bring detection and treatment to underserved communities, and invest in research to protect and restore vision.

“Glaucoma can steal a person’s sight before they even know they have it. By the time symptoms appear, the damage may be irreversible,” said Congresswoman Frederica S. Wilson (FL-24). “A screening could change the course of someone’s life, but too many people face gaps in coverage or cannot afford the care they need. My bill would help families detect glaucoma earlier, get treatment sooner, and hold on to the independence that comes with their sight.”

Approximately 4.22 million Americans were living with glaucoma in 2022, and about half of people with the disease are unaware they have it. Although Medicare covers screenings for certain people at high risk, federal law does not uniformly require glaucoma screening coverage across Medicaid, private health plans, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program.

Key Provisions of the Glaucoma Vision Act of 2026

Expands screening coverage across major health plans. The bill would require glaucoma screening coverage for eligible people with private insurance, Medicaid, and Federal Employees Health Benefits coverage. It would also eliminate applicable Medicare Part B cost sharing for screenings furnished to eligible people. The coverage provisions would generally take effect in 2027.

Reaches people at higher risk. Eligible individuals include adults age 40 or older who identify as having African, Hispanic/Latino, or Asian ancestry, or who have a clinical risk factor such as diabetes, a family history of glaucoma, elevated eye pressure, myopia, certain blood pressure conditions, or chronic corticosteroid use. Adults age 60 or older would also qualify.

Brings screening and treatment into underserved communities. Through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vision Health Initiative, the bill would establish competitive grants for free or low-cost screenings and follow-up treatment for uninsured and underinsured people at high risk. Grants could also support community education, mobile screening units, care coordination, and disease surveillance. Projects serving racial and ethnic minority communities and other underserved populations with a high burden of vision loss would receive priority. The bill authorizes $10 million for these activities across fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

Advances research on glaucoma and optic nerve damage. The bill would authorize $10 million across fiscal years 2027 and 2028 for National Eye Institute research, including work on optic nerve repair, neuroprotection, gene therapies, and approaches to preserving or restoring vision.

“No one should lose their sight because glaucoma went undetected. The Glaucoma Vision Act of 2026 would expand screening coverage, invest in community detection programs, and support vital research to improve treatment and prevent vision loss. The Academy applauds Representative Wilson for introducing this important legislation and advancing eye health for all Americans,” said Michael Repka, MD, MBA, Medical Director for Governmental Affairs, American Academy of Ophthalmology.

“The impacts of untreated glaucoma extend beyond the individual, leading to emotional and psychological challenges for patients and their families. It can also diminish independence and contribute to substantial economic costs at both local and national levels through decreased productivity and increased health care demands. Given that there is currently no cure, proactive screening and prompt treatment are essential to reduce incidents of preventable blindness. Congresswoman Wilson’s legislation addresses this critical public health issue by increasing access to early glaucoma screening and investing in public health and research. Put together, these initiatives aim to protect vision, maintain independence, and mitigate the long-term personal and economic effects associated with this silent, irreversible disease. Prevent Blindness applauds Rep. Wilson’s efforts to promote early detection, preserve sight, and improve the health and well-being of our communities,” said Karen Allison, MD, MBA, FACS, Associate Professor of Clinical Ophthalmology at the Flaum Eye Institute, University of Rochester Medical Center; Prevent Blindness Board of Directors member; and Prevent Blindness Public Health & Science Committee Co-Chair.

“Protecting someone’s vision protects their ability to work, care for their family, and move through the world on their own terms,” said Congresswoman Frederica S. Wilson (FL-24). “We have the knowledge to catch glaucoma earlier. We must make sure people have the opportunity to act on it.”

Cosponsors of this bill are Reps. Joyce Beatty (OH-3), Sanford Bishop (GA-2), Troy Carter (LA-2), Yvette Clarke (NY-9), Emanuel Cleaver (MO-5), Jasmine Crockett (TX-30), Lois Frankel (FL-22), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-7), Jonathan L. Jackson (IL-1), Robin Kelly (IL-2), Lucy McBath (GA-6), Jennifer McClellan (VA-4), LaMonica McIver (NJ-10), Christian D. Menefee (TX-18), Kweisi Mfume (MD-7), Jerrold Nadler (NY-12), Terri Sewell (AL-7), Brad Sherman (CA-32), Shri Thanedar (MI-13), Bennie Thompson (MS-2), Nydia Velázquez (NY-7), Maxine Waters (CA-43), Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12), and Nikema Williams (GA-5), as well as Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-AL).

Organizations supporting this bill are the American Academy of Ophthalmology, American Glaucoma Society, American Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgery, Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology, Alliance for Vision Research, Cornea Society, Macula Society, Foundation Fighting Blindness, and Prevent Blindness.
title: Rep. Wilson Introduces Glaucoma Vision Act to Expand Screenings and Prevent Vision Loss

Today, Congresswoman Janelle Bynum (OR-05) released the following statement following the alleged use of a racial slur during a recent Oregon high school football game.

“Football is supposed to be about teamwork, healthy competition, and kids getting the chance to do something they love,” said Rep. Bynum. “A kid should be able to put on their jersey, take the field, and worry about the next play – not whether someone is going to attack them on their race, sex, religion, or any other distinguishing feature. A racial slur is not trash talk. It’s not a rivalry. It’s straight up racist. In the state legislature, I sponsored legislation to make sure incidents like this couldn’t just be swept under the rug. We can’t ask young people to speak up and then fail them when they do. We need to teach our kids that reporting incidents like these will be taken seriously, investigated, and appropriately addressed based on the findings.

“The Oregon School Activities Association must step up and double down on eliminating these incidents. I have no tolerance for our kids being harmed in competition by racial slurs. And I have no patience for mealy-mouthed adults who throw their hands up and say there’s nothing we can do. If OSAA does not act, the governor and legislature should consider taking up a stronger set of sanctions sooner, rather than later.”

As a state legislator, Congresswoman Bynum introduced HB 3409, requiring a process for reporting and responding to harassment and hateful language during school sports and activities. The legislation was in response to a 2019 racial slur incident at Parkrose High School during a girls varsity basketball game, as well as other reports from students around the state.

Today, the Department of War announces the award of twenty-six Defense Community Infrastructure Program (DCIP) grants from the Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation, totaling approximately $230 million in federal awards. DCIP is a competitive program for states, territories, and communities to undertake infrastructure enhancements to support the mission assurance of a military installation, military family quality of life, installation resiliency, and/or the training of cadets at independent "covered educational institutions," that benefits their local installations.
On August 4, 2026, the Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations, and Environment instructed the Office of Local Defense Community Cooperation to invite grant applications for projects based on a competitive ranking of all proposed projects in response to an April 17, 2026, DCIP Notice of Funding Opportunity.

"The Fiscal Year 2026 awards deliver historic funding to the Defense Community Infrastructure Program, driving critical infrastructure upgrades that directly strengthen military installations nationwide," said Mr. Dale Marks, Assistant Secretary of War for Energy, Installations, and Environment. Press Statement

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

September 23, 2026

Foreign commercial birth tourism networks have exploited the U.S. immigration system to sell U.S. citizenship for profit. These networks advertise and coach foreign nationals to lie on U.S. visa applications and collect tens of thousands of dollars to arrange births on American soil for the sole purpose of obtaining U.S. citizenship.

Today, I am announcing a new visa restriction policy under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. This policy targets individuals who knowingly engage in, have engaged in, or facilitate birth tourism to the United States, including owners, operators, and managers of commercial birth tourism facilitation networks, visa “fixers” who coach applicants to commit fraud, foreign medical providers who knowingly abet and facilitate such travel and the fraudulent use of our Medicaid system, and other individuals who support, abet, and enable commercial birth tourism.

The Trump Administration is using every tool at our disposal to defend the integrity of U.S. citizenship, protect American public benefits and U.S. taxpayers from exploitation, and safeguard our national security. By restricting visa issuance of those who both engage in and profit from this fraud, we are sending a clear message: The United States will not allow foreigners to exploit our immigration system and violate the sanctity of U.S. citizenship.

This visa restriction policy is pursuant to Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Certain family members may also be covered by these restrictions.

Tags
title: Protecting the Sanctity of U.S. Citizenship: A New Visa Restriction Policy for Those Who Engage in or Facilitate Birth Tourism

WASHINGTON D.C. – U.S. Representative Greg Stanton (AZ-04) led Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego and Reps. Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03) and Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07) in pressing Interior Secretary Doug Burgum for answers after reporting revealed that the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) is weighing data center-related proposals on federal public land.

The proposals, not previously made public, show that the Trump administration is considering 12 data center and data center-related infrastructure projects covering more than 17,600 acres of federal public land across Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming. Four of the proposed data centers and related infrastructure projects are in Arizona, and they would span more than 3,000 acres of federal public land here.

In the letter, the lawmakers raise questions about how these data center proposals were fast-tracked by Trump’s Executive Order 14318; how the projects will be implemented; and what this could mean for environmental reviews, public oversight, and Arizona’s water and energy resources.

“Arizonans are entitled to transparency and robust public review as BLM considers such developments on our federal lands,” the lawmakers write.

The delegation requested a congressional briefing before any of the proposed Arizona projects move forward. By October 2, 2026, they demand that Secretary Burgum provide information on:

All data center proposals and candidate parcels under consideration in Arizona;

The permitting and environmental review required for each proposal, including whether BLM intends to use categorical exclusions or other expedited procedures;

Opportunities for public participation and consultation with Tribal governments, local governments and elected officials; and

The projected water demand, water source and peak electric load associated with each proposed project.

The letter to DOI Secretary Burgum is HERE.
title: Stanton Leads Arizona Democrats in Pressing Trump Administration for Answers on Proposed Data Center on Public Lands

text:
Remarks

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Palace Hotel

New York City, New York

September 23, 2026

SECRETARY RUBIO: Okay, go ahead.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, what were the U.S. demands with the Iranians yesterday, and was there any discussion of return to the MOU, or have the terms changed for the United States in terms —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, yesterday’s conversation was with some of the mediators involved in that process, and I don’t want to characterize it as one direction or another. I think it’s a pretty clear understanding of what this – remember everything here, at its core, the number one issue – the President highlighted this yesterday in his speech before the world – Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. Everything emanates from that.

We understand the straits is an issue. The southern lane of the straits is open. Every day more and more barrels of oil are flowing through there. And they’re open, thanks to the efforts of the United States military that’s both defending shipping and has removed mines. And that trend will continue. Meanwhile, the only blockade in the Hormuz Straits is the one we’ve imposed on Iran because they keep firing on ships and they continue to do so as early as this morning. There was another launch, so – on shipping. So, we’ll continue to defend. We’ll continue to hold the straits open. So that’s an issue.

But the core issue here is that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. We make that point in every interaction with them. Beyond that, I would say that – I don’t want to characterize these meetings because these – if there’s going to be a deal with Iran, it’s not going to happen at a press conference. It’s going to involve a lot of hard work over a period of time, and it will engage and involve mediators as well.

So as the President said, he’s open to a deal. The President’s open, still to this moment, to making a deal with Iran that allows Iran to be what it should be, which is a great and prosperous country. But if they continue to insist on the desire for a nuclear weapon, their support for proxies in the region that – their support of terrorism – they’re the world’s leading sponsor of terrorism – then we’re going to have big problems with them. And the President has a number of options available to him, including the ones he’s already taken, which is to impose severe and growing economic costs. But he also has some military options, upon which I won’t speculate.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, the President said that freedom will come to Cuba.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes.

QUESTION: How will that happen? In the past you’ve said that it’ll collapse on its own, but –

SECRETARY RUBIO: Who has said that?

QUESTION: Well, the administration has said that the regime –

SECRETARY RUBIO: No, no. Look —

QUESTION: The President has said it.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, look. The Cuban revolution – want to answer. I know your question. The Cuban revolution has failed. It has failed for 60-something years. It is a failure now. And I think there’s acknowledgment within the Cuban system that the revolution has failed. The question is what replaces it or what – and they have an opportunity to make changes; they have an opportunity to begin to put their country on an irreversible trajectory towards progress and a better future. And that involves both political and economic freedom, no doubt about it.

And so, we’ll be reengaged in that portfolio. We’ll do – we’re open to measures moving forward that begin that process of change. And it will be a process that will not be easy. We’ve seen these transitions happen historically throughout the world. They don’t happen overnight. They don’t happen immediately. You don’t reverse 60-something years of mismanagement, corruption, and incompetence in six months.

But I do think that Cuba has a golden opportunity to place itself on an irreversible path towards a better future, and we are prepared to be helpful in that regard if they’re open to it, obviously. Right now, I mean, Cuba still – at least the people that speak on behalf of the government and led by people who, at least publicly, are quite recalcitrant. But the reality of their situation is things are not going to get better in Cuba without them making very substantial changes.

QUESTION: But could it involve something like Venezuela, changing the regime with some military extraction? There’s an indictment against the former president. There are other actions. Would you rule that out?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Look, first of all, the United States – and I say this – this is a general answer, not even specific towards Cuba – if there was a threat to the national security of the United States, the President has both the power and the obligation to address it. That’s just my general statement, not just Cuba-specific. That said, our preference always is to deal with these things in a – I don’t want to call it diplomatic, but in a negotiated way, in a political way, in a way in which progress is made through substantial changes to a country that don’t involve the use of military force.

So, I’m not going to speculate beyond that, and I’m certainly not going to threaten anything. I’m just going to tell you that Cuba and its leaders, or the people that are in charge of its government now, have an opportunity to begin the process of forever positively changing that country. And it’s an opportunity that they should take, and I’m hopefully that they will. I’m not confident that they will, but I’m hopeful that they will. And we stand prepared to contribute towards that.

Obviously, there are some individuals in that regime with whom we can never work because their hands are stained in blood. But there are people there that I believe that you could work with, if they are willing to put the country on a path towards political and economic freedom and the process that will get us to that ultimate goal, although that’ll take some time to get there.

QUESTION: The President said yesterday that he believed that the U.S. would strike a deal with Iran after the midterm elections. What indications do you have from the Iranians that that might be true?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think the Iranians misread our system. I think the Iranians are under this illusion that Democrats are going to win in November, and the President will no longer be able to do things against them. I just don’t think they understand our system very well. Other countries do, but they don’t seem to. In our system of government, obviously Congress – the legislative branch is a very important branch of government. I served in it for 14 years, so I understand its powers, but also understand its limitations.

When it comes to the national security of our country, when it comes to the imposition of both sanctions and the use of military force, the President has extraordinary powers. Every president does. He’s the Commander in Chief, both constitutional and otherwise, to be able to carry out those functions.

So, I think that the Iranians are fundamentally misreading our political system. And I think the President made it very clear yesterday: for him, the Iranian issue is not a political issue. It is the fact that for generations now – for almost 50 years – every American president and, frankly, every country in the world for the most part, agrees that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. But ultimately, no one ever does anything about it, and he’s going to do something about it. And he’s doing something about it. And it comes at a price and at a cost, there’s no doubt about it. But the cost of not doing something about it is substantially higher, especially for future generations.

QUESTION: President Macron yesterday —

SECRETARY RUBIO: You have to hold your own mic? Oh, man, budget cuts. You gotta get it crushed. Okay.

QUESTION: Small details. President Macron yesterday spoke about a descent into – a return to the law of the jungle and spoke about this idea of an erosion of international norms, something that other leaders here seem to (inaudible). I wonder what you thought of that, and also whether the language of annihilation of countries gives people grounds to think that that’s happening.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I didn’t see President Macron’s speech. We saw him – the President saw him briefly, I guess, the night before that speech, so I don’t know what he’s referring to. Yeah, look, I mean, the international system is not in good shape right now. These international norms people talk about – I think the limits of international norms is your national interest. At the end of the day – the President and I have reflected this, going back to the very beginning – the view of this administration is that the number one obligation of every government is the national interest of their country.

And so, the United States will – obviously, we see the utility in the international system. We’re here. We’ve argued – I think the President has said – that the United Nations, for example, has tremendous potential, but it’s not living up to it because it’s lost its – and I think multiple leaders – a very curious thing, and I think something you guys should point to is multiple leaders pointed to the fact that the international system is failing. And it’s failing because it has grown beyond its mandate. It has grown beyond its intent. It’s involved in all kinds of things it shouldn’t be involved in, and it’s unable to solve virtually any major conflict in the world. So, I think there’s unanimity and consensus here in this gathering and broadly that the international system’s broken. But it’s broken because it broke itself. It needs to be brought back to its proper focus and its proper role.

And yeah, it would be great if we had a functional international system, for example, that could deal with a war between Thailand and Cambodia that occurred, or the potential conflict between India and Pakistan, or what’s going in the DRC and Rwanda, or what’s going on in Sudan, or what’s going on with Iran in the straits. Right now, we don’t seem to have a functional international system that can address it. And in the absence of that, nation-states will act in their national interest.

I will say this to you – and I want to be clear because this is not an attack on the international system. But at the end of the day, the United States will always act – at least as long President Trump is in office – we will always act in the national interest of our country, not in the interest of the international order. We will never put the international order above the interest of the United States.

QUESTION: But just the language of annihilation —

QUESTION: Any indication coming out of the GCC multi-lat if there is any sort of coordination or consensus going forward among allies as to how to deal with Iran?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I think there’s consensus that the straits need to be open and free without attack. I think there’s consensus that what’s happening with the Houthis and in Yemen is deeply problematic. I think there’s a consensus that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. And I think writ large, you’ve seen a lot of support from many of those countries for the sanctions and the economic costs that the United States is imposing.

So, we work in coordinated – very closely with these countries for a variety of reasons: A, because they’re in a position to be very helpful on the economic front and there’s an expectation that they will live up to that; and the other is because they are directly threatened. At the end of the day, the one thing you will find in the region is that virtually every country in the region is facing the threat of some Iranian proxy that has for years – not for the last few months, for years – threatened the safety and security of these countries. And on that, there’s very strong consensus that Iran is a malign force in the region.

QUESTION: (Off-mike.)

SECRETARY RUBIO: Go ahead. Hi.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Who are you are with? I’m sorry.

SECRETARY RUBIO: I like praise. We don’t get praise always, you know that, guys.

Go ahead. Yes.

QUESTION: Yeah. There’s a great deal of praise coming.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah.

QUESTION: So how do you see evolving role of Serbia as the American strategic partner? And how specifically do you intend to deepen that partnership?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we intend to – and we already have. I mean, we’ve taken steps in this administration to grow closer in our interactions. I know we’ve already had individuals from the State Department and other government agencies visit there. Hopefully I’ll have an opportunity to visit as well. Obviously, Serbia’s tied up in some issues that are potentially problematic and explosive and that there’s international interest on. But it is a strategic partnership that we’d like to deepen, and intend to do so, as we manage some of the potential issues that might emerge as a – that I know deeply involve them as well.

QUESTION: A question from German press?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Go ahead, yes.

QUESTION: Back on the subject of Cuba, how far along are the opportunities —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Ah, how come I always get the Cuba questions? (Laughter.) Go ahead. I’m sorry. Yeah, yeah. I know. I know. I get you.

QUESTION: (Inaudible.)

SECRETARY RUBIO: I know. It’s a joke.

QUESTION: How far along are the opportunities for American privatization of Cuban industrial sectors? And have you personally seen any of the proposals for U.S. business interest to own or operate on the island that would satisfy some of the administration’s goals?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, first of all, here’s – it’s actually a good question about – the question is on Cuba and American private sector. What people have to understand is unlike some other parts of the world, U.S. policy towards Cuba is codified in law, in statute, by Helms-Burton. So, there are substantial limitations to what any American company can do in Cuba, because Helms-Burton – a law that was passed by Congress and is on the books – limits it. It makes certain conditions have to be met in order for that commercial interaction to happen.

Now, do I believe that American business interests could play a positive role in a future Cuba in which its economy is free and open and people are allowed to self-employ or work for whoever they want? Sure, of course. We’re the largest economy in the world. I also think, by the way, that one of the huge opportunities that Cuba has is that it has a very large expatriate community of Cuban Americans and Cubans living in other parts of the world that could contribute greatly, the diaspora that could contribute greatly to Cuba’s future. And there are also companies from other parts of the world that could contribute as well.

The fundamental challenge in Cuba, and what keeps companies – forget about American companies for a moment, because obviously they’re impeded by – from some investments by Helms-Burton. What keeps – Cuba can do trade and commerce with any country in the world they want, outside the United States. The reason why they don’t is because why would I invest – giving you an example – why I, businessperson from whatever, Spain – why would I invest $10 million in Cuba if two years from now they just decide on their own to change the rules, take it from me, and keep the money and never pay me back? And that’s happened over and over and over in Cuba. Even now, as they announce these reforms, everyone’s saying, well, these things are just on paper; (a) you have to implement them, and (b) you have to keep them. So, certainty is the problem, and there’s simply no legitimacy or credibility that this regime will ever live up to these conditions, because they never have before. So, that ultimately is an impediment.

But to answer your question, have I reviewed any of these, well, look, people are always pitching things. I’m aware that there are some companies and individuals and others that would love to be involved in Cuba’s economic future. But right now, that’s not possible; (a) it’s not feasible, because of Helms-Burton, and also because of the lack of certainty about its future. No one is going to invest in Cuba under their current governance model. They’re just not going to do it. Which is why I always go back to it’s not just about political freedom, which is incredibly important, but it is about having a governance model on that island that give the private sector confidence that if they invest, they’re going to make their money back with a profit and have – not have it taken from them and never get paid back.

QUESTION: On Russia. On Russia, Mr. Secretary.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah.

QUESTION: (Inaudible) your meeting with Lavrov.

SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m very partial to the people that have to own their own mikes. Go ahead.

QUESTION: (Laughter.) We do own everything here.

SECRETARY RUBIO: All right.

QUESTION: Did you find that the Russians are at all interested in a energy ceasefire, as Zelenskyy has been proposing?

SECRETARY RUBIO: I think both sides have expressed an interested in some limited ceasefire that involved grain and energy. Obviously, that won’t be easy either, because – but it’s something that both sides have expressed some interest in. I think President Zelenskyy has done so publicly; did it with us yesterday, did it I think in interviews over the last few hours. And so obviously, look, that’s something that might – it doesn’t solve the war, but it does I think in some ways potentially alleviate some of the global pressures that are being felt as a result of that.

So that’s something we’re always open to exploring. It’s been a feature of every conversation that we’ve had with them. It was a feature of the Witkoff-Kushner meeting in Moscow and in Kyiv; it was a feature of our conversation with President Zelenskyy yesterday. And it’s something that if we can play a constructive role in making happen, we’d be very open to. Again, recognizing it doesn’t end the war, but it does deal with something – and maybe it can serve as the baseline or a platform for a broader agreement. Ultimately, we all want this war to end, and that’s the one thing about Russia and Ukraine I will say, is that war is not going to end on the battlefield. That war is going to end – I think everyone acknowledges – with a negotiated agreement. And we all understand that. And the sooner we can reach that agreement, the less things will be destroyed, and the less people are going to die on both sides. That’s what the President wants.

QUESTION: On the hybrid attacks – on the hybrid attacks —

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, if I could ask you about the meeting that President Trump had last night with acting President Delcy Rodríguez, can you tell us about what was discussed, what you —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah.

QUESTION: What you shared, what she shared?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, it was a short meeting, but it was an important meeting, and obviously there are three things that were discussed that are important. Number one is, look, at the end – I’ll go back to what we said from the very beginning. Venezuela is dealing with almost 20-something years of destruction, okay, economic and otherwise. And then you add to that probably the worst earthquake in the region maybe ever, according to seismologists; I am not a seismologist, so I rely on their expertise on it, but certainly a very devastating one. And by the way, an earthquake that could have been far worse had it hit inland versus on the coast, but it was very bad. The full death toll is still not known. And as you saw, they struggled to respond to it because they had not invested in the mechanisms to do so as a government.

So, Venezuela has a lot of problems. They have probably the world’s largest sovereign debt that has to be restructured. They have an economy that is still suffering from the remnants of kleptocracy and graft, and the fact that that regime was held together, the glue that held the regime together was corruption and the fact that individuals tied to government got sweetheart deals that they have to disentangle from. There’s 8 million Venezuelans living abroad, many of whom would desire to come back to Venezuela, live there, invest there, rebuild their businesses there, but they need to have confidence that that’s going to happen.

So, there’s a lot that needs to be fixed in order for Venezuela to be successful. So, we discussed the steps that remain to make that happen, and debt restructuring is key to that. Obviously, we want to be helpful in that regard; it has to be done in the right way.

The second and equally important is there has to be a political transition process, which is underway. Leadership from the 2015 National Assembly have been engaged now in regular talks with the interim authorities to create the groundwork and rebuild the institutions necessary in order to have free and fair elections in Venezuela, which is critical.

What we don’t want to see, right – what we want to see is not only that you have free and fair elections but that you have an enduring republic. What would threaten an enduring republic in Venezuela would be that someone is elected and they inherit a complete catastrophe, economic and social, and then the whole project is endangered because now anything can happen. So, we want to do two things at the same time. We want to help them rebuild their economy – not perfect, but certainly to a level of stability that allows an elected government to succeed – and second is build back all the things necessary in order to truly have free and fair elections.

What are the things that are required for that to happen? You need media. You need media coverage. You need – candidates need to be able to communicate with the public, and there have been positive steps in that regard. In just the last two weeks – underreported fact, but a number of independent Venezuelan outlets that had not been allowed to broadcast in Venezuela for almost seven years are now broadcasting in Venezuela. If you watch some of these opposition figures, they do press conferences, and there are literally 50 microphones on the table. If you had gone there two years ago, there would have been three microphones at the table.

You need to rebuild political parties. Many of the leaders of these parties are still abroad. It’s not just María Corina, who’s a very brave woman, but there are other people that are abroad. These parties need the opportunity to rebuild, to organize, to become not protest movements but political movements.

You need to have an electoral process that people have confidence in – in essence, are the votes going to be accurately counted and accurately reported. So, you need to have authorities that govern elections so people have confidence that those elections are real.

So, we made that point: that in the end, for this project to be successful, it culminates in a free and fair election in which the leaders of that country have the credibility that the private sector will have confidence in. But obviously we also need at the same time to work on the economic conditions that need to be improved, because if you have societal breakdown, if you have economic crisis in Venezuela, it not only endangers elections, it endangers the survival of a democracy there, which is ultimately what we want to see in Venezuela: a stable democracy with a functional economy that allows its people to have prosperity and allows many of the millions of Venezuelans who have had to leave the opportunity to go back and live in their country again, invest in their country again, participate in their country again.

QUESTION: On Ukraine, Secretary. Ukraine says its refinery strikes inside Russia is aimed at targeting revenues that are the main income source for Russia. Why lean on a country that’s been invaded and not invader?

SECRETARY RUBIO: What is that? I’m sorry, the —

QUESTION: That the U.S. asks Ukraine to stop targeting Russian energy sites.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, there’s two energy —

QUESTION: Why are you not asking Russia? They’re doing it first. It would appear to be —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, we – I mean, how do you know we haven’t asked Russia to stop.

QUESTION: No, just —

SECRETARY RUBIO: So, look, I mean, when you talk to energy, for the Russian side, the energy strikes they’re facing are refineries and their oil and gas. For the Ukrainian side, energy means their electrical grid and going into winter with a fear of losing the electric grid. So, when you talk about energy, it means two things to different people. And what complicates it further is that energy strikes are at the core of the tactical pursuit that both sides are – the Ukrainians are inflicting pain on the Russians by hitting their energy sector, which is a revenue source. The Russian side is inflicting pain on the Ukrainian side by targeting their electric grid, especially as we head into winter.

So, there’s the challenge, is that both sides have identified energy as a strategic objective of their war aims. But it’s having a global impact in the case of oil and gas and it’s having a very real and immediate impact on life in Ukraine, especially these threats to it. So that’s why it’s not easy overnight to just say let’s reach an agreement, but it’s something that I think is worth investing in, trying to make that happen, because I think it would be beneficial to the world and beneficial to both countries. I think if you ask President Zelenskyy, he would argue that the ability to protect his electric grid is at the core of their interests, and we – so that’s something that we can help achieve through a deal, and obviously the Russian side is facing strikes it has not seen before, deep in Russian territory and against key industries.

So that’s what makes making a deal on that limited basis difficult. But it also is the reason why it’s so important that we try. So, we’ll try, and I think we’re prepared to play a positive role if we can in making that come about.

Yes, ma’am. Right there.

QUESTION: You said – Mr. Secretary, you said that Russia is ready to —

QUESTION: In the U.S.’s trilateral meeting with Japan and South Korea, there were concerns raised about supply chain stability in the Taiwan Strait. Will the U.S. raise these matters at the upcoming summit with China?

And on the arms sale to Taiwan, when do you think that will be finalized?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, which arms sales to Taiwan? I’m sorry.

QUESTION: The one that’s still pending.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, again, look, I mean, this is – this – people think this is just – we view arms sales through the limited vacuum of the one particular place. A lot of this also involves balancing our industrial capacity and our military-industrial base. We’re not in the – and I don’t – this is not about Taiwan in specific, but when we sell something, that means we don’t have it anymore. We can get it in the future, but we don’t have it now. So anytime we do any sales – not to Taiwan, to anybody – it is always balanced against what are our own needs in different parts of the world and whether we can afford to sell something, because we may need it for ourselves. So that’s going through that process.

On the broader issue of supply chains, the United States – we have this trilateral going on with South Korea and Japan, and I think we’ve had those meetings now – well, we had three in the last four months or four in the last three months, and we continue to engage. It’s a very useful forum. And I think when you look at one of the shared interests that both Japan and Korea are advanced technological economies, so they have the same supply chain concerns that we do, and I think they’re excellent partners. We’ve signed memorandums of understanding with them. We’re cooperating with them jointly on a number of other places in the world where we can work together to improve supply chain security.

Obviously, supply chain issues are global in nature. The need to diversify our supply chains is a global international imperative that we share with many countries. It’s been at the core of our policy, not just as we engage with South Korea and Japan but as we engage with the world.

And I imagine that those issues will also be discussed in our interactions with the Chinese because it’s been at the – much of our interactions with China over the last year have been largely focused on the trade portfolio, which Secretary Bessent and Greer are handling, and supply chains are at the core of that trade portfolio. So, there’s no doubt that issue will be raised. But in the meantime, we’re going to continue to work with partner nations around the world to diversify our supply chains on everything, not just critical minerals but on everything – pharmaceuticals, everything else.

QUESTION: On Germany, Mr. Secretary. On Germany —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Germany, okay.

QUESTION: Yes . I’m with German press (inaudible). There’s been an increase of hybrid attacks recently on Europe and on Germany. Specifically, there was just a drone that was stocked with explosives. Is that a conversation you’re having with Secretary Lavrov? And also, can the – can Europe and Germany count on you —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah. First of all, let me be clear, because she’s asking what all was raised. Like, these meetings don’t work really well with anybody if I leave the meeting and run out and tell the media this is what we talked about, that’s what we talked about. I’m not trying to be secretive with you.

QUESTION: No, no, that’s fine.

SECRETARY RUBIO: I’m just telling you, let’s be frank here, I mean, these meetings don’t work well.

Now, let me comment generally. Yeah, one of the concerns we have, among many, about the war between Russia and Ukraine is that could metastasize and spread into other places, that it could grow into somewhere else, be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding – some pilot went the wrong way and all of a sudden you’ve got active combat. These things are of concern. We raise that in multiple meetings with multiple countries because it’s of real concern. I mean, these things – these are how things sometimes get out of control is that war metastasizes to some other part of the world or some other country. So, yeah, we’re concerned about it. We watch reports carefully and we raise them with the right people at the right levels.

Go. You haven’t had a question.

QUESTION: Hi. Could I come back to the situation in the Middle East and Yemen, specifically? What is – is the President and you prepared to do more against the Houthis because the situation there on the other side —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, well, so I’m not going to get into a discussion about the tactical options available to the President. As I’ve said and we’ve said and I’ll say again, we have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement. We don’t like what’s happening, obviously. It’s very disturbing. I’m happy to see that the Saudis were able to restart the pipeline again, which is critical for their economy and also critical for the global economy. We think these strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East – they weren’t just attacked by the Houthis. They were probably also attacked by Shia militias in Iraq who are an Iranian proxy.

Every time you guys ask me a question about the Middle East, it goes back to someone supported by Iran. Let’s just be clear here. The Iranian system, the Iranian regime, actively supports organizations in the Middle East who target infrastructure – energy infrastructure – and civilians. Okay? Civilians. They attack, for example, diplomatic facilities. Unheard of that you would bomb or attack, for example, our embassy in Kuwait. That’s a diplomatic facility that was deliberately targeted – it wasn’t hit by shrapnel – all being done by people that are sponsored by the Iranians.

So, they are a malign force in the region, and that’s why the region understands it. But going back to your question about Saudi Arabia, they are a strategic defense partner. The U.S. has made commitments to them. We will live up to those commitments. We are living up to those commitments now. And that’s all I’ll say about it. Obviously, the President has many options available to him.

Okay. In the back, right there. Yes, ma’am.

QUESTION: Hi. Ros Jordan, Al Jazeera English. You put out a pretty dismal statement yesterday about the situation in Sudan, and your administration basically said the SAF and RSF are not credible interlocutors to try to find peace. Who are the parties that can try to bring peace to Sudan? What is the U.S. Government doing to try to move this war from just continuing —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yeah, we have a team of people that work Sudan, like full time. It’s a very frustrating thing. We’ve had agreements both at various gatherings around the world. We’ve had people agree to things, sign to things, and the commitments are never met. I want to be frank. I mean, we all recognize that what’s happening in Sudan would not be happening were it not for external actors supporting one side or the other, and it’s growing increasingly frustrating. We have engaged in it. We have participated in it. Us, the UK, other countries have tried to play a role in furthering this.

But every time it seems like we’re making progress towards something that at a minimum – like, we would love to see a permanent peace agreement, but at a minimum we would like to see the opening of humanitarian zones, because the humanitarian calamity there is very significant. And every time it seems like we’re on the verge of making progress, one side or the other will back off because they think they’re winning or they think they could win. And there are external actors. I’m not going to single them out. You know who they are. I don’t want to create any more friction than there needs to be created. But that war and that conflict and that crisis would not be happening were it not for the active participation of external actors that are feeding one side of that conflict or another.

So, I would say that, ultimately, until those external actors are prepared to use and influence and pressure their respective proxies to live up to the commitments that they’re making, we’re not going to make progress. And so, we are raising this in every forum and in every setting possible. We would like to see a positive outcome there. At minimum, we would like to see the humanitarian situation addressed because it’s catastrophic and horrifying. Aid groups cannot go into these active combat zones. Both sides have made commitments to allowing certain areas to be safe, and then they don’t live up to it. But we would like to see the war ultimately solved, but that doesn’t mean we’re going to stop – but if we can at least achieve the humanitarian achievement in the short term, we can build upon that, and that’s what we’ve tried to do. But it’s been frustrating, as I said, because of external players that are involved. Okay?

QUESTION: (Off-mike.)

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, are you confident that Prime Minister al-Zaidi can control the militias in the timeline he set out, and is there any discussion about extending the U.S. final withdrawal timeline?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, there’s been no discussion on extending the timeline. We – I met with him, and then the President saw him briefly last night as well and had this conversation. Look, we have zero doubt of his commitment to doing this. We understand it’s a massive challenge and a difficult challenge. I think he’s achieved certain things. At least three militias have disarmed and have basically joined the national government. There are a couple, at least one in particular, that has not been as forthcoming. And we recognize that’s going to be a real challenge that he’s going to have on his hands. And as we’ve told him, we want him to succeed. We think he gives the world and Iraq the best chance to succeed. I think he has the right intentions; I think he has the right motivations. He’s very intelligent and a very willing partner in this regard, and we’re doing to do everything we can to help him achieve the results.

And we know it will not be easy; we know it will be difficult. And we want to help him to achieve it, because nothing would be more important for Iraq than to deal with this and to bring all the arms in that country under the control of its national government, and you don’t have these independent forces operating and balkanizing the country. So, we’re going to do everything we can to help him, because we do believe strongly that he wants this to work, and we want it to work for him, and we’ll do everything we can to help him succeed.

QUESTION: Did he ask you to extend your presence there?

SECRETARY RUBIO: No.

QUESTION: (Off-mike.)

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, were the talks particularly substantive yesterday, or was it a bit —

SECRETARY RUBIO: Which talks?

QUESTION: For some of the talks with Witkoff and Kushner on – and the Iranian counterparts, well, was it – was in in-depth or was it just surface level? And if it was surface level —

SECRETARY RUBIO: I wouldn’t – first, I’m not going to characterize the talks one way or the other. The readout and the reporting that I have on it, which is pretty deep, is that basically it was a continuation of conversations that have occurred in the past with people involved in those conversations. But again, as I’ve highlighted in the context of whether it’s Foreign Minister Lavrov or any of these other meetings, it’s our experience that sometimes – oftentimes – it is not constructive or productive for us to leave them and come out and tell you the blow-by-blow of what happened for a variety of different reasons.

Again, the United States always remains open to talking to almost anyone in the world about a conflict or a crisis or some disagreement that we may have. So, if there’s an opportunity to exchange ideas and messages, we will. And that’s what largely yesterday was. It was positive in that regard. But ultimately, I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough, but at the same time, I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.

QUESTION: (Off-mike.)

SECRETARY RUBIO: You right there in the back. Yes, sir.

QUESTION: Mr. Secretary, your former colleague —

QUESTION: Secretary, is there a desire on the U.S. – on the U.S. side for another Trump-Putin summit?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Is there a desire for?

QUESTION: Another summit between President Trump and President Putin.

SECRETARY RUBIO: That hasn’t been discussed. I mean, look, the President of the United States – this President – is willing to engage and meet with virtually anyone. His view of the world, which I think maybe from a traditional political standpoint people don’t understand it, but I do, coming from the world he comes from – he’s a businessman who relies more on common sense than he does on political orthodoxy – is if you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings but nothing happens. In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with.

So, we’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the President but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept. There’s an opportunity in December if that happens. If there’s another opportunity for them to meet and there’s a purpose behind the meeting, that would be good. Contact: Jin.Choi@mail.house.gov
WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Monday, Congresswoman Nanette Barragán (CA-44) welcomed the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s issuance of a direct final rule, which updates federal regulations to clarify scientifically appropriate non-animal methods can be used to evaluate the safety of drugs and biological products before they are tested in humans.
The FDA’s action follows bipartisan congressional efforts led by Rep. Barragán and Rep. Buddy Carter (R-Ga.) to ensure the agency fully implements the authority Congress established through the FDA Modernization Act 2.0. In April 2025, Barragán and Carter introduced the FDA Modernization Act 3.0, legislation requiring FDA to publish a final rule updating its regulations to reflect the availability of non-animal testing methods. The bill was cosponsored by Reps. Diana Harshbarger (R-Tenn.), Troy Carter (D-La.), Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), and Vern Buchanan (R-Fla.).
“Modern science is giving us better tools to understand how medicines affect people, and our laws and regulations need to keep pace,” said Congresswoman Nanette Barragán. “I’m proud to have worked across the aisle to advance the FDA Modernization Act 3.0 and help ensure that FDA’s regulations reflect the scientific tools available today. This action is an important step toward giving researchers greater flexibility to use validated methods that can improve drug development while maintaining rigorous safety standards.”
“This is a long-delayed but highly consequential move by FDA to bring drug-development regulations into the 21st century,” said Wayne Pacelle, president of the Center for a Humane Economy and Animal Wellness Action. “The agency knocking down outdated regulatory language propping up ineffective animal testing strategies put new methods rooted in human biology. Over time, we’ll see better, safer, less costly drugs that help people struggling with disease.”
The FDA’s new rule updates terminology and removes language that could suggest animal testing is the only acceptable approach for generating safety information for human drugs and biological products. The agency said the rule recognizes a broader range of approaches, including methods involving human cells, organs-on-chips, computer models, and other New Approach Methodologies (NAMs).
The rule does not prohibit animal studies or change existing evidentiary standards. FDA stated that non-animal methods may be used when they are adequately validated and appropriate for the product and regulatory question.
The FDA’s action is being issued as a direct final rule and is subject to public comment.
The full bill text can be found HERE.
###
title: Rep. Barragán Applauds FDA Action Advancing Non-Animal Testing Methods

Washington, D.C. – In case you missed it: On September 16, 2026, the House passed H.R. 9497, the bipartisan Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) of 2026, to authorize critical water infrastructure projects and programs for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE). Specifically, McClellan applauded the inclusion of three initiatives that she requested to authorize water resource studies and water infrastructure projects in the Commonwealth of Virginia.

“The Water Resources Development Act of 2026 serves as proof that Congress can still work together on a bipartisan basis to tangibly better the lives of local communities and environments for generations to come. This bill will significantly strengthen our waterways, ports, harbors and critical water infrastructure across the country, and those in Virginia and beyond will feel its effects,” said Congresswoman McClellan. “I am especially grateful to see that priorities I championed to serve Virginia communities have been included in this year’s WRDA. From proactively managing flood control for the James and Appomattox Rivers, to increasing funding for the Chesapeake Bay Oyster Recovery Program, to delivering $25,000,000 to improve water infrastructure for Henrico County in my district, these projects advance comprehensive quality-of-life improvements and ensure that the health, safety and well-being of our inland waterways and the people who live around them remain a priority.”

The 2026 WRDA includes water resources infrastructure and projects of the USACE. Since 2014, Congress has enacted a WRDA every two years to help improve water resources infrastructure. WRDA-authorized projects of the Corps are locally-driven projects that deliver regional and national benefits. The 2026 WRDA will enact and bolster numerous projects in the Commonwealth of Virginia, including three of McClellan’s submissions involving the Petersburg, Chesapeake Bay and Henrico County areas.

The three initiatives McClellan successfully requested included in the 2026 WRDA are as follows:

James River Flood Risk Management Feasibility Study. This project modification would include additional portions of the Appomattox River to an existing feasibility study and add flood risk management as a purpose to better support water infrastructure in the region and mitigate potential damages incurred by flooding. The Appomattox River has not been dredged since 1949. This initiative would authorize dredging along the Appomattox River including at Petersburg to restore navigational capacity of the Appomattox River by removing the significant sedimentation that has accumulated in the Petersburg Harbor and portions downstream. The bill also authorizes additional flood-management activities to address frequent flooding in Petersburg and other localities along the Appomattox River. Failure to dredge the river and subsequent sediment buildup prevents the River from navigational uses and further impedes the function of the City’s storm sewer outfalls. Over 67 acres of the City’s urban downtown suffer from frequent flooding due to inadequate river conveyance.

Chesapeake Bay Oyster Recovery Program Authorization Increase. The purpose of the Chesapeake Bay Native Oyster Recovery Program in Virginia is the restoration and rehabilitation of reef habitat to provide for self-sustaining native oyster populations and associated fish and wildlife habitat within the Chesapeake Bay watershed in Virginia. According to USACE, the program is currently about $38 million short of its authorized cap of $120 million. Scheduled work over the next two years in Virginia and Maryland would bring the total close to the $120 million cap before the next anticipated WRDA. Without an increase in program authorization in the 2026 WRDA, USACE’s ability to prepare needed oyster recovery work in the Chesapeake Bay could be imperiled. This initiative would make a $30 million increase in program authorization to address anticipated oyster recovery work in the Bay through 2030.

East End Water Transmission Main (Design) for Henrico County. This project entails the preliminary and final design of approximately 70,000 LF of 42” water transmission main (WTM) and will deliver $25 million to Henrico County for the purposes of completing this project. This new WTM is intended to run from an existing 48” WTM in the central part of the County to an existing 36” WTM located in the east end of the County. This would improve resilience in Henrico’s water supply system, allowing continued transmission of clean water from the western side of the County to the eastern side in the event that Richmond experiences another water treatment facility failure, similar to what occurred at the beginning of 2025.
title: McClellan Celebrates Securing Three Virginia Initiatives in Water Resources Development Act of 2026

Congressmen Pocan and Langworthy Introduce Bipartisan COMPACT Act to End Taxpayer-Funded Biomedical Testing on Dogs and Cats
The most comprehensive legislation to prevent companion animals from barbaric testing practices
WASHINGTON, DC -
Congressmen Mark Pocan (WI-02) and Congressman Nick Langworthy (NY-23) today announced the introduction of the Companion Animal Protection Against Cruel Testing (COMPACT) Act, the most comprehensive legislation in history to modernize federally funded biomedical research and end inhumane testing practices on dogs and cats.
The legislation was announced at a press conference in Washington with the nation’s leading animal wellness organizations and rescue beagles released from Ridglan Farms in Wisconsin, which drew national attention and closure following revelations of widespread abuse.
The COMPACT Act prohibits the use of federal public-health research funds for biomedical research involving live dogs and cats while protecting animals currently in research facilities and preserving flexibility for genuine national emergencies. The legislation, developed with input from the medical and bioscience community, comes as advances in biomedical science have created alternatives to traditional animal testing, including in vitro systems, computational modeling and other non-animal technologies.
“What happened at Ridglan Farms was a wake-up call for our community and for the country,” said Congressman Mark Pocan. “We saw thousands of beagles confined in inhumane conditions and bred for research, and we saw what was possible when people came together to demand change.
“This is a nonpartisan issue, and I am glad to work with Congressman Langworthy to build on that progress with the COMPACT Act,” Pocan continued. “For years, our federal research agencies have worked on reducing animal testing and turning to more humane and effective alternatives, and this legislation takes the important next step in modernizing our federally funded research and protecting animals.”
“The horrific abuse and barbaric treatment of beagles uncovered inside research facilities like Ridglan Farms and Marshall Biosciences has outraged Americans from every corner of the country and political spectrum,” said Congressman Nick Langworthy. “Dogs and cats are companion animals and part of the family for millions of Americans; they should never have to endure inhumane suffering, particularly at expense to taxpayers and when science has evolved to develop more effective research methods. This is the most comprehensive legislation to date that moves our federal research system forward to better outcomes, while protecting innocent animals. I’m proud to work with my colleague, Congressman Pocan, on this thoughtful, bipartisan legislation.”
The COMPACT Act would:
- Prohibit the use of federal funds administered by the Department of Health and Human Services and relevant subagencies for research involving live dogs and cats, including grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, fellowships, training awards and other federal funding mechanisms.
- Protect and rehome animals currently being used for biomedical testing, giving them an opportunity for life outside research facilities.
- Establish strong compliance and oversight mechanisms and provide law enforcement with tools to protect dogs and cats from taxpayer-funded experimentation.
- Increase transparency and accountability at HHS through an annual agency report and a Government Accountability Office review three years after enactment.
- Provide clear standards and transition provisions for research institutions, giving facilities certainty as they move toward modern, non-animal research methods.
The legislation is endorsed by the nation’s leading animal rights and wellness advocacy groups, including the Animal Wellness Action, White Coat Waste Project, Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine, Humane World for Animals, Humane World Action Fund, the Beagle Freedom Project, PETA, and Save the Dogs.
“We are past due to close out the long, painful era of government-funded invasive testing on beagles and on cats,” said Wayne Pacelle, president of Animal Wellness Action and the Center for a Humane Economy. “In a world of predictive AI, organoids, and so many other biomedical innovations, American taxpayers need not subsidize ineffective experiments on animals widely recognized as beloved members of our families. We thank Congressman Langworthy and Pocan for leading an effort to usher in cruelty-free medicines and animal-free science.”
"This is a common-sense Act long overdue in recognizing that dogs and cats deserve protection. The federal government should not be funding experimentation on them when they belong in homes. Beagle Freedom Project stands at the ready to place these animals in loving homes," said Shannon Keith, president and founder.
“The COMPACT Act is a long-overdue step toward ending the use of dogs and cats in animal research” said Blair Eagleson, legislative affairs fellow at the Animal Legal Defense Fund. “By ensuring that the Department of Health and Human Services will not fund these practices, we are protecting our companion animals and encouraging biomedical research to prioritize humane methods. The Animal Legal Defense Fund thanks Congressman Langworthy for championing this cause to protect future dogs and cats from being used for research and offering a pathway to find loving homes for those who are currently suffering in labs.”
“Dogs and cats belong in homes, not laboratories, and taxpayer dollars should support research that better translates to human health. The COMPACT Act will help direct federal agencies toward research that benefits people and spares animals. The Physicians Committee commends Rep. Langworthy and Rep. Pocan for recognizing that protecting animals and improving science go hand in hand,” said Janine McCarthy, director of research policy at the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine.
Wayne Hsiung of Save the Dogs said, "Americans have been paying $40 million a year to fund cruel experiments on dogs and most have no idea. The COMPACT Act finally puts taxpayers back in control of their own money, and ends a program the science stopped justifying long ago. We're grateful to Rep. Langworthy for leading this fight."
“Americans should not be forced to pay for painful, deadly experiments on dogs and cats when modern, reliable, human-relevant research methods are available,” said Kathy Guillermo, PETA senior vice president. “The bipartisan COMPACT Act will help move federally funded research into the 21st century while protecting dogs and cats from suffering in laboratories. PETA applauds Representatives Langworthy and Pocan for their leadership and urges Congress to swiftly pass this commonsense legislation.”
title: Congressmen Pocan and Langworthy Introduce Bipartisan COMPACT Act to End Taxpayer-Funded Biomedical Testing on Dogs and Cats

“Americans have a right to know how data center projects affect their communities, and that is why we need to ban non-disclosure agreements between data center developers and government officials or agencies. WASHINGTON – The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) today announced country-specific in-quota allocations of the tariff-rate quota (TRQ) for imported raw cane sugar for Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 (October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027).
TRQs allow countries to export specified quantities of a product to the United States at a relatively low tariff, but subject all imports of the product above a pre-determined threshold to a higher tariff.
On July 14, 2026, the Administrator of the Foreign Agricultural Service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced the establishment of the in-quota quantity for raw cane sugar for FY 2027. The in-quota quantity for the TRQ on raw cane sugar for FY 2027 is 1,117,195 metric tons raw value (MTRV), which is the minimum amount to which the United States is committed under the World Trade Organization (WTO) Agreement. On July 24, 2026, USTR provided notice of country-by-country allocations for 1,061,202 MTRV of the FY 2027 in-quota quantity of the WTO TRQ for imported raw cane sugar. See 91 FR 46822. The U.S. Trade Representative is allocating the remaining quantity of 55,993 MTRV to the following countries in the amounts specified below.
The allocations of the raw cane sugar WTO TRQ to countries that are net importers of sugar are conditioned on receipt of the appropriate verifications of origin. Certificates of quota eligibility must accompany imports from any country for which an allocation has been provided.
In-quota quantities of the FY 2027 TRQ for imported raw cane sugar may enter the United States as of October 1, 2026.
Conversion factor: 1 metric ton = 1.10231125 short tons.

U.S. Representative Rick Larsen (WA-02) joined 110 House Democrats in a letter to tech industry leaders last Friday demanding that all data center construction follow strict guardrails to protect consumers from electricity and water price hikes.

“Data center projects and the energy systems and infrastructure that support them must be built and operated responsibly with a commitment to high-quality construction, good jobs, strong environmental stewardship, and strong partnerships with the communities they serve,” wrote the Members.

The lawmakers stated that they would oppose new data center construction projects that failed to incorporate strong labor standards, negotiate community benefits agreements with local leaders, and mitigate impacts on local air quality, drinking water and utilities costs for residents.

“At a time when the nation's power grid, roads, bridges, schools, and other public infrastructure require significant investment, data center development must strengthen rather than strain, these systems,” the Members continued. “Developers must also invest responsibly in grid infrastructure, including new generation and grid upgrades, to protect ratepayers from bearing the costs of data center projects' energy needs.”

The full text of the letter to tech industry leaders can be read here.

Larsen Holds Data Centers Accountable

Last week, Rep. Larsen voted for legislation to protect families from higher electricity bills because of data centers in their communities (the Ratepayers Protection Act). Rep. Larsen also cosponsors the Big Ugly Tax Breaks for Data Centers Act to roll back tax breaks for large AI data centers in Republicans’ Big Ugly Law.

Rep. Larsen supports tough, upfront restrictions on data centers:

No high electric bills for local families and small businesses;

No federal tax breaks;

No construction without community approval and union labor;

Data centers must pay their fair share to connect to and use the grid; and

Data centers must use closed loop water systems.

A one-pager on Rep. Larsen’s work to hold data centers accountable can be found here.
title: Larsen Fights for Guardrails on Data Centers

PITTSBURGH, PA – SEPTEMBER 23, 2026 — Yesterday, Congresswoman Summer L. Lee (PA-12) joined Bethlehem Haven, ACTION-Housing, Pittsburgh Mercy, local elected officials, housing advocates, community partners, and residents to celebrate the grand opening of Uptown Flats, a new 34-unit affordable permanent supportive housing community in Pittsburgh’s Uptown neighborhood.

Previously, Rep. Lee joined project partners for the groundbreaking of Uptown Flats in October 2024 and returned Tuesday as the nearly decade-long effort officially welcomed residents home.

“Today, we get to celebrate 34 new homes, 34 new beginnings, and one more example of what Western Pennsylvania can build when we put people first,” said Rep. Lee. “For someone coming out of homelessness, or a senior, veteran, or person with a disability who has spent too long wondering where they are going to lay their head at night, this kind of stability can mean the difference between surviving and finally having some room to breathe. Housing is a human right, and Uptown Flats shows us what that can actually look like in practice.”

Developed through a partnership between Bethlehem Haven and ACTION-Housing, Uptown Flats includes 11 studio apartments, 16 one-bedroom apartments, and seven two-bedroom apartments designed to provide safe, stable housing for people exiting homelessness and residents with disabilities and other special needs. All 34 apartments receive Project-Based Section 8 rental assistance, helping ensure residents can afford their homes based on their income. The development also provides accessible units, community spaces, and on-site supportive services to help residents build long-term stability.

The more than $22 million development brought together federal, state, county, city, nonprofit, and private investment, including federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits and HOME-ARP funding. The development sits along Pittsburgh’s Bus Rapid Transit corridor and includes accessible housing designed for residents with mobility, hearing, and visual disabilities.

Rep. Lee has made expanding access to safe, affordable housing a central part of her work in Congress. Earlier this year, shesecured $3 million to help Allegheny County create affordable rental homes dedicated to people exiting homelessness anddelivered another $1 million to help convert vacant Downtown Pittsburgh office space into affordable housing. Last year, Rep. Lee alsojoined Allegheny County Executive Sara Innamorato to celebrate the “500 in 500” initiative, which helped house more than 600 people experiencing homelessness and identified hundreds of affordable housing units across the county.

In Congress, Rep. Lee helped reintroduce theStop Wall Street Landlords Act to curb large institutional investors’ ability to use taxpayer subsidies to buy up single-family homes and theHOMES Act to restrict tax breaks for large corporate investors purchasing local housing. Her affordable housing agenda also includes expanding federal rental assistance, strengthening tenant protections, preserving affordable housing, and preventing displacement and homelessness.
